questions: Which everyday liquids in the scene are acids?
segments.say: Acids and alkalis around you. Lemon juice and vinegar are acids; soap and baking soda are alkalis. Chemists sort them all on one number line: the pH scale. Point at two items and tell your partner which side of the scale each one sits on.

questions: How many times stronger is each pH step?
segments.say: The pH scale ladder. The scale runs from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral in the middle. Watch the ladder: each step away from 7 is ten times stronger, so small pH differences are big acidity differences. Quick check: how many times more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5?

questions: What decides whether a solution is acidic or alkaline?
segments.say: What pH is really about: ions. Watch the particles: acids release H+ ions in water and alkalis release OH- ions. Whichever ion is in excess decides the pH. Tell your partner: more H+ means the pH goes which way?

questions: What do the H+ and OH- ions form when they pair up?
What is left over after neutralisation?
segments.say: Neutralisation: a worked example. Mix the acid and the alkali and watch the H+ and OH- ions pair up to make water. The leftover ions form a salt: acid plus alkali always gives salt plus water. Now try the ion question on your worksheet.

questions: What happens to blue litmus in an acid?
What does no colour change tell you?
segments.say: The litmus test. Blue litmus turns red in acid, red litmus turns blue in alkali, and no change means neutral. Watch both papers change and say the rule with me: blue to red, acid ahead.

questions: Which salt name comes from sulfuric acid?
Why does the acid decide the salt name?
segments.say: Naming the salt. The salt takes its name from the acid: hydrochloric gives a chloride, nitric a nitrate, sulfuric a sulfate. Chant the three pairs with your partner, then name the salt made from nitric acid.

questions: What does a weak acid do with its hydrogen ions?
Is vinegar an acid? How do you know?
segments.say: A common mistake: all acids are strong. It is tempting to treat every acid as fully ionised and dangerous, but watch the weak acid here: it only partly releases its hydrogen ions. Vinegar is still acidic, just not strong. Say it with me: weak is about ion release, not about being harmless.

questions: What happens to the pH at the equivalence point?
Where on the curve must the indicator change colour?
segments.say: The titration curve: watch for the jump. Base goes in drop by drop and the curve draws itself: slow at first, then a single drop leaps the pH from 4 to 10. That jump is the equivalence point, and an indicator must change colour somewhere on it. Before we finish, work through the trap section of your student notes in pairs, check the worksheet answers, then do the exit ticket on your own.
segments.watchFor: All acids are strong acids. Listen for students who treat vinegar as not an acid, or who call every acid fully ionised. Send them back to scene 7: Weak acids only partly release their hydrogen ions: vinegar is still acidic, just not strong.
